1. What is the discharge time of the capacitor?
2. What is the average value of the discharge current?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a power source labeled E, connected to the upper contact a; the middle branch is capacitor C, whose upper end can be connected to a or b through switch S, and whose lower end is connected to the common lower node; the right branch is inductor L, whose upper end is connected to contact b, and whose lower end is also connected to the common lower node. Therefore, when the switch is at a, the capacitor is charged by the power source; after the switch is moved from a to b, the power source is disconnected, and capacitor C and inductor L form an ideal LC circuit. Reasoning: The electromotive force of the power source is E_i, so when the switch was originally at a, the initial charge of the capacitor is Q0 = C E_i. After moving to b, the LC circuit satisfies L d²q/dt² + q/C = 0, with angular frequency ω = 1/√(LC). Taking the initial condition q(0)=Q0, one obtains q(t)=Q0 cos(ωt). When the capacitor is completely discharged for the first time, q=0, therefore cos(ωt)=0, giving t = π/(2ω) = (π/2)√(LC). The total amount of charge passing through the circuit during this discharge time is Q0 = C E_i, so the magnitude of the average discharge current is I_avg = Q0/t = C E_i / [(π/2)√(LC)] = (2E_i/π)√(C/L).

method.method_draft: First describe the circuit image: the left branch is a battery labeled E connected to contact a; the middle branch is a capacitor C whose upper plate is controlled by switch S; the right branch is an inductor L connected to contact b, with a common bottom node. Thus with S at a the capacitor is charged by the battery, and after switching to b the battery is disconnected and the capacitor forms an ideal LC loop with the inductor. From the text, take the supply emf as E_i, capacitance C, and inductance L. Use Q0 = C E_i for the initial capacitor charge. For the discharge after switching to b, write the LC equation q/C + L dI/dt = 0 with I = -dq/dt, giving q(t)=Q0 cos(t/sqrt(LC)). Complete discharge first means q=0, so t = pi/(2 omega)= (pi/2)sqrt(LC). The average discharge current is total charge transported divided by this time: I_avg = Q0/t = C E_i /[(pi/2)sqrt(LC)] = (2E_i/pi)sqrt(C/L).

\frac{q^2}{2C}+\frac12 L i^2=\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}。

raw_record.original_question:
The electromotive force of the power supply is \( E_{i} \), the capacitance of the capacitor is \( C \), and the inductance of the coil is \( L \). When the switch \( S \) is turned from \( a \) to \( b \), the capacitor discharges completely after a period of time.

1. What is the discharge time of the capacitor?
2. What is the average value of the discharge current?
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: On the left side of the figure is a power source labeled E, connected to the upper contact a; the middle branch is capacitor C, whose upper end can be connected to a or b through switch S, and whose lower end is connected to the common lower node; the right branch is inductor L, whose upper end is connected to contact b, and whose lower end is also connected to the common lower node. Therefore, when the switch is at a, the capacitor is charged by the power source; after the switch is moved from a to b, the power source is disconnected, and capacitor C and inductor L form an ideal LC circuit.

Reasoning: The electromotive force of the power source is E_i, so when the switch was originally at a, the initial charge of the capacitor is Q0 = C E_i. After moving to b, the LC circuit satisfies L d²q/dt² + q/C = 0, with angular frequency ω = 1/√(LC). Taking the initial condition q(0)=Q0, one obtains q(t)=Q0 cos(ωt). When the capacitor is completely discharged for the first time, q=0, therefore cos(ωt)=0, giving t = π/(2ω) = (π/2)√(LC). The total amount of charge passing through the circuit during this discharge time is Q0 = C E_i, so the magnitude of the average discharge current is I_avg = Q0/t = C E_i / [(π/2)√(LC)] = (2E_i/π)√(C/L).
